core: The working definition of cash flow: the increase or decrease in the amount of money a business has — the cash generated or consumed in a given time period — attributed to CFI
Inflows and outflows: money coming in versus money going out, each with original examples
The three activity types — operating, investing, and financing — each with one line and an original example; the statement of cash flows is owned by the accounting subject and referenced only
Cash flow versus profit: a business can show profit and still run out of cash, with an original example
Cash flow timing: when money moves matters, with the honest note that collections and payments run on their own schedules
Why managers watch cash flow: paying bills, payroll, and suppliers depends on cash, not profit
The honest framing: cash flow is the pulse of the business — the real-time measure of whether money is actually moving

claims.claim: Cash flow is the increase or decrease in the amount of money a business, institution, or individual has — the amount of cash generated or consumed in a given time period.
Cash flow is used to assess liquidity — how well a company can meet its short-term financial obligations — and is one of the most important metrics in finance.
Income and profit are based on accrual accounting principles, so a company's net income can be materially different from its cash flow.

Under the cash method of accounting, transactions are recorded only when cash flows — cash inflows and outflows are tracked as they occur; the cash method is commonly used by small businesses that deal primarily in cash transactions.
Under accrual accounting, revenues and expenses are recorded in the period in which they are earned or incurred, no matter when cash receipts or payments occur.
Cash can be received a significant amount of time after the initial transaction, which is why accrual accounting takes the timing of transactions into account.

Cash flows from operating activities arise from the activities a business uses to produce net income — cash sources from sales and cash used to purchase inventory and to pay operating expenses such as salaries and utilities.

Cash flows from investing activities are cash transactions related to a business's investments in long-term assets — payments for the purchase of land, buildings, and equipment, and cash receipts from selling them.

Cash flows from financing activities are cash transactions related to the business raising money from debt or stock, or repaying it — proceeds from notes or bonds, issuance of capital stock, dividend payments, and principal repayments.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The term 'cash flow' is used loosely and can refer to several different measures.
positions: CFI notes that 'cash flow' can mean any of several things — cash from operating activities, free cash flow to equity, free cash flow to the firm, or the net change in cash — so the term must be clarified in context.

This lesson uses the general working definition (money moving into and out of a business over a period) and names the three activity types only at the level needed for a foundations lesson, leaving statement-level reporting to the accounting subject.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which picture is more truthful: profit or cash?
positions: OpenStax's Principles of Finance explains that accrual accounting is theoretically preferable because it matches revenues and expenses to the period in which they occur, giving a fuller picture of performance.
CFI emphasizes that investors and business operators care deeply about cash flow because it is the lifeblood of a company and measures the ability to meet short-term obligations.
This lesson holds both together honestly: profit tells you whether the business model works; cash flow tells you whether the business can keep running while it proves that.
